newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy budget can't cut welfare alone-Prodi adviser.
newsitem.headline: Italy budget can't cut welfare alone-Prodi adviser.

text.p: Italy's 1998 budget cannot rely on pruning pensions and welfare payments alone if cuts in the public sector deficit of 25 trillion are to be achieved, said Paolo Onofri, an economic adviser to Premier Romano Prodi.
"We cannot make all the budgetary adjustment next year on the shoulders of the welfare system," Onofri told a news conference.
The government is expected to reveal the exact size of the 1998 budget package when it unveils a three year rolling programme of economic targets later this month.

Italy is committed to reducing the ratio between its budget deficit and the gross domestic product to the three percent target for first wave membership of Europe's planned single currency from 6.7 percent in 1996.
Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said in Brussels on Monday that he was aiming to cut the public deficit to below three percent in 1998.
Newspapers have reported that the 1998 budget, which the government has to formulate by the end of September, will aim to cut around 25 trillion lire from the deficit.

"If we assume that the budget correction for next year is of the order of 25 trillion lire, we can draw no more than seven or eight trillion lire from the pensions system and the general welfare system," said Onofri.
Onofri recently completed a study of Italy's system of welfare benefits and made detailed recommendations for carrying out structural reforms.

"The rest of the amount of the correction must be found in the other items of the budget, not to a large extent in the revenue side but to a definitely larger extent in the other primary expenditures," he added.
Onofri said identified these as "general public administration expenditures for goods and services and for wages and salaries, for transfers to firms and for contributions to production."
He said the government would have to impose hefty spending cuts on Italy's loss-making and inefficient postal and railway systems.
The government is also believed to be considering increases in value added taxes as a means of raising extra revenue.
